h1:
Sa Kaeo History Trip
Following the Khmer Temple Trail in 2 Days
intro: Most people know Sa Kaeo as a border province with the big Rong Kluea market, but it's actually home to some of the oldest Khmer temples in Thailand. This stretch of land was part of an ancient Khmer civilization route that predates Angkor Wat. This plan lays out a Khmer temple trail over 2 days, 1 night, from Sdok Kok Thom, which holds the longest inscription chronicling the Khmer royal line, to the pink hilltop temple of Khao Noi, where the oldest dated inscription in Thailand was found. We've paced it so you can actually see everything without burning out, with real distances and how to get there in 2026.
chips: 🛕 Khmer temples older than Angkor Wat

blocks.html: If you like traveling with a story behind it, Sa Kaeo is a province people overlook but it hides plenty. Several Khmer temples here were built from the 7th century onward, hundreds of years before Cambodia's Angkor Wat, and one of them holds the oldest dated stone inscription ever found in Thailand. We've split this history trail into 2 days: day one heads to Sdok Kok Thom in Khok Sung district, and day two climbs the pink Khao Noi temple at Aranyaprathet in the morning, then stops at a museum to round out the story before heading home.

One thing to be straight about: many of the temples in Sa Kaeo sit close to the Thai–Cambodian border, especially Sdok Kok Thom, which is roughly 1 kilometer from the border, and the temples around Ta Phraya district. The border situation can change from time to time, so always check the news and any provincial or district announcements before you set off. If you plan to cross the border or get near the boundary, prepare your documents and ask local officials for clear guidance.

blocks.text: Why Sa Kaeo is a Khmer temple province

blocks.html: Sa Kaeo sits on an ancient transport route linking the Korat Plateau with the Khmer capital of Angkor, which made it a place for stone sanctuaries even before the Angkor period. Temples here reflect both Hinduism and Mahayana Buddhism, from early brick temples like the pink Khao Noi to the sandstone and laterite temples of the golden age such as Sdok Kok Thom. The best part is that crowds are still thin here, so you can walk around quietly without competing for photo spots.

items: Much older than Angkor Wat — the pink Khao Noi was first built around the 7th century, while Angkor Wat dates to the 12th century

Inscriptions of national importance — the Khao Noi inscription records the Maha Saka year 559 (AD 637), the oldest dated inscription in Thailand, while Sdok Kok Thom holds the longest known inscription tracing the Khmer royal line
Still uncrowded — unlike Phimai or Phanom Rung, the Khmer temples in Sa Kaeo are still quiet, ideal if you like peaceful travel

blocks.text: Day 1 — Hitting Sdok Kok Thom, Khok Sung district

blocks.html: Day one heads to the northeast of the province in Khok Sung district. Sdok Kok Thom sits about 80 kilometers from Sa Kaeo town, roughly an hour and a half by car, or closer if you start from Aranyaprathet at around 35 kilometers. The final stretch is rural road through rice fields, so we recommend driving your own car or renting one, since public transport doesn't reach the temple itself.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Eastern Thailand's largest stone temple + the Khmer dynasty inscription

items.note: Fill up on fuel and grab some drinking water to take along, as the final stretch is rural road without many shops. Leaving early means you'll walk the temple before the sun gets harsh.

items.activity: Sdok Kok Thom Historical Park visitor center
items.note: Start at the information center before entering the temple itself. There's a video room and exhibits explaining the history, inscriptions and restoration, which helps you understand what you'll see outside. Free entry.

The largest sandstone and laterite Khmer temple in eastern Thailand, built around AD 1052 in the reign of King Udayadityavarman II. It has a central prang, two libraries and a gallery. Give yourself about an hour and a half to take it slow.

items.activity: See the inscription site and ancient baray
items.note: The Sdok Kok Thom inscription chronicles several successive Khmer kings, a key piece of ancient Khmer history. Around the temple you'll also find traces of a baray, an ancient reservoir, to walk and explore.

items.activity: Lunch in Khok Sung district / on the way back
items.note: There's a decent choice of stir-fry shops and noodle stalls in the district town, with local prices around 50–70 THB a plate. Refuel before carrying on.

Stay overnight in Aranyaprathet since it's close to day two's sights. Hotels and resorts in the district town start around 500–900 THB a night. Save your energy for an early hill climb the next morning.
Find dinner in Aranyaprathet town, with everything from street food to Khmer-Thai dishes. It's the kind of border-town atmosphere you won't get in Bangkok.

blocks.title: Day one tip
blocks.html: Sdok Kok Thom is about 1 kilometer from the border. It's usually open during office hours, but when the border situation is tense there may be announcements closing or limiting access. Before you go, check the Sdok Kok Thom Historical Park page or the Sa Kaeo provincial public relations office to be sure, so you don't make the trip for nothing.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Morning climb up the pink Khao Noi + the museum

blocks.html: On day two you'll want to wake up early, because the highlight is the pink Khao Noi temple set on a hilltop facing east. When the morning light hits the orange-red brick, people of old saw it as pink, and that's how it got its name. The temple is inside Wat Khao Noi Si Chomphu in Khlong Nam Sai subdistrict, about 12 kilometers south of Aranyaprathet town.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: A hilltop temple, the oldest dated inscription in Thailand, and the museum

items.activity: Leave Aranyaprathet for Wat Khao Noi Si Chomphu
items.note: About a 20–30 minute drive to the foot of the hill. Going early gets you soft light and cooler air, and the 254-step staircase is far more comfortable than later in the morning.

items.activity: Climb up the pink Khao Noi temple
items.note: Khao Noi rises about 130 meters from the ground, with 254 steps to the top, or if your legs aren't up to it there's a concrete road behind the hill you can drive part of the way up. The temple is open around 08.30–16.00, but the hill area can be reached earlier. The temple is built of brick laid without mortar, originally three towers, with the central prang and two earthen mounds remaining.

items.activity: Take in the view and the story of the Khao Noi inscription
items.note: From the top you can see fields and the distant Cambodian hills. This is where the Khao Noi inscription was found, recording the Maha Saka year 559, equivalent to AD 637, the oldest dated inscription in Thailand. Imagine someone carving this stone about 1,400 years ago.

items.activity: Head down + coffee break in Aranyaprathet
items.note: Come down and find a cafe or coffee shop in Aranyaprathet town to rest your legs for a bit before moving on. The sun starts to bite around now, so resting in the shade for a while is more comfortable.

items.activity: Stop at Rong Kluea Market (if you have time)
items.note: Aranyaprathet's big border market, good for browsing cheap secondhand goods, clothes and bags. It's a break from the temple theme before closing the trip with the museum. If shopping isn't your thing, you can skip it.

Prachinburi is on the way back. The museum holds artifacts from the Khmer temples around Sa Kaeo and Prachinburi, including lintels, deity images and pieces from Khao Lon temple. It's a fitting way to wrap up the Khmer story. Closed Monday and Tuesday, so check the hours before you go.

blocks.title: What to know about the climb
blocks.html: The 254 steps are fairly steep, so wear sneakers or shoes with grip and carry water up with you. In the rainy season the steps can get slippery, so take extra care. Before 9 a.m. is the most comfortable time to climb, since the sun is still soft and there are fewer people.

blocks.text: Other Khmer temples in Sa Kaeo to add on

blocks.html: If you have more than 2 days, or you want to dig deeper into the Khmer trail, Sa Kaeo has several more temples to extend the route. But some sit deep in, close to the border, so always check the situation and ask locals before heading in.

items.name: Prasat Khao Lon
items.blurb: A brick temple in Ta Phraya district, built around the 11th century. It's the source of a lintel that was once taken out of the country and later reclaimed. The temple sits close to the border, so check on safety before you go.

items.name: Prachinburi National Museum
items.blurb: Holds artifacts from Khmer temples across eastern Thailand, including lintels, deity images and pieces from Khao Lon. A good spot to grasp the bigger picture before or after visiting the actual temples.

blocks.text: Rough budget per person (2 days, 1 night)

items: Temple entry — most are free or charge a small upkeep fee. The Sdok Kok Thom information center is free
Aranyaprathet lodging — hotels and resorts start around 500–900 THB a night
Fuel / car rental — the route totals around 200–250 km, with fuel around 400–600 THB per trip (split among the group)
Food — local meals at 50–70 THB a plate, around 200–300 THB a day
Prachinburi museum — entry is a few tens of baht

blocks.title: The most comfortable time to visit
blocks.html: November to February is cool and dry, ideal for walking the temples and climbing the hill. Avoid the rainy season (June–September), when the Khao Noi steps get slippery and some rural roads have potholes. March to May is very hot, so if you go you'll need to start very early and pack plenty of water.

blocks.text: What to know about the border before you go

items: Many temples, especially Sdok Kok Thom and the temples around Ta Phraya, sit close to the Thai–Cambodian border
The border situation can change, so always check the news and provincial / district announcements before you go
If you plan to cross at the Khlong Luek–Poipet checkpoint, have your passport and documents ready, and ask about the latest conditions at the checkpoint
Respect the area, follow the signs and officials' guidance, and don't stray off the designated route
Save emergency contact numbers and tell people at home where you're going, just in case

faq.q: How many days do you need for the Sa Kaeo Khmer temples?
faq.a: If you cover the two main sites, Sdok Kok Thom and the pink Khao Noi, 2 days and 1 night is just right and unhurried. Day one hits Sdok Kok Thom in Khok Sung, day two climbs the pink Khao Noi in the morning and stops at the museum. If you want to add Khao Lon temple or deeper sites, an extra day makes it more relaxed.

faq.q: How do you get to Sdok Kok Thom, is there public transport?
faq.a: It's in Khok Sung district, about 80 kilometers from Sa Kaeo town or around 35 kilometers from Aranyaprathet. Public transport doesn't reach the temple itself, so we recommend driving your own car or renting one. The final stretch is rural road through rice fields, so fill up on fuel and bring drinking water.

faq.q: Why is the Khao Noi temple called pink?
faq.a: Because the temple is built of orange-red brick and faces east, so when the morning sun hits it, from a distance it looks pink. Locals took to calling it the pink Khao Noi temple. If you want to see this tone clearly, go in the morning.

faq.q: How old are the Sa Kaeo temples, are they really older than Angkor Wat?
faq.a: Much older. The pink Khao Noi temple was first built around the 7th century, and it holds an inscription dated to AD 637, the oldest dated inscription in Thailand, while Cambodia's Angkor Wat was built around the 12th century, so it's older by several hundred years.

faq.q: Is it safe to visit temples near the Sa Kaeo border?
faq.a: They're usually open during office hours, but because they sit close to the Thai–Cambodian border, the situation can change from time to time. Before you go, check the news and provincial or district announcements. If you plan to cross the border, prepare your documents and always ask local officials first.
